3.2 NPV, IRR and Capital Budgeting

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

Net present value

Section titled “Net present value”

Companies decide every day whether to build a new plant, buy new equipment or launch a new product. These long-term investment decisions are called capital budgeting. What they have in common: pay now, receive later.

0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money gives the way to compare: present value. Write the cash flow in year ttt as CtC_tCt​ (C0C_0C0​ is usually negative: the initial investment) and the discount rate as rrr. The project’s net present value (NPV) is

NPV=∑t=0TCt(1+r)t\text{NPV} = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}NPV=t=0∑T​(1+r)tCt​​

The NPV rule: accept if the NPV is positive, reject if it is negative; among projects of which only one can be chosen, choose the one with the largest NPV. A positive NPV means the project creates more value than it uses; shareholders’ wealth rises by exactly the NPV.

The discount rate rrr should be the cost of capital: the expected return investors could earn by putting their money elsewhere at the same risk. It is an opportunity cost, not the rate at which the company actually borrows. The riskier the project, the higher the cost of capital (Stage 4 discusses how to estimate it).

Check C1
A company can borrow all the money a project needs from a bank at 6%, while investments of the same risk are expected to earn 10%. Which discount rate should be used for the project's NPV?
The loan rate is the price of the bank's risk. A bank loan is repaid first and is less risky than the project's cash flows, so its rate is not the price of the project's risk.
Averaging has no basis: the discount rate should reflect the risk of the project's own cash flows, whatever the source of the money.
The project's cash flows are risky estimates, not certain amounts; discounting at the risk-free rate ignores that risk.

Which cash flows to include

Section titled “Which cash flows to include”

NPV should include only the cash flows that change because of the project (incremental cash flows): the difference between doing it and not doing it.

  • Sunk costs are excluded: money already spent that cannot be recovered whether or not the project goes ahead, such as completed market research (sunk cost).
  • Opportunity costs are included: if the project uses an existing resource that could otherwise be sold or rented out, the income given up is a cost of the project.
  • Side effects are included: if a new product takes sales from the company’s existing products (cannibalization), the lost cash flows count against the new project; if it raises sales of other products, that counts too.
  • Working capital: the inventory and receivables the project needs tie up money; this is a cash outflow at the start and is recovered at the end.
  • Taxes: depreciation is not itself a cash outflow, but it lowers taxable profit and so lowers the tax paid (Exercises Question 5). The US federal corporate income tax rate is 21% (since 2018, under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act).
  • Nominal and real must match: discount nominal cash flows at a nominal rate and real cash flows at a real rate (Fisher equation).
Check C2
When evaluating a new product project, which of the following should not be included in the project's cash flows?
If the land were not used for the project, it could be sold for cash. Using it gives up that money, which is an opportunity cost of the project.
The lost cash flow of existing products happens because of the project, so it is part of the project's incremental cash flow.
The extra inventory ties up cash, and it is needed only because of the project.

The internal rate of return

Section titled “The internal rate of return”

The discount rate that makes NPV equal to zero is the internal rate of return (IRR):

∑t=0TCt(1+IRR)t=0\sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{C_t}{(1 + \text{IRR})^t} = 0t=0∑T​(1+IRR)tCt​​=0

The IRR usually has to be found by trial or with a calculator. It is intuitive: what “rate of return” does the project itself earn? The IRR rule: accept if the IRR is above the cost of capital.

Viewing NPV as a function of the discount rate and plotting it gives the NPV profile. For a conventional project, which pays out first and receives later, the higher the rate the lower the NPV, and the curve crosses the horizontal axis only once, at the IRR. So the NPV is positive whenever the cost of capital is below the IRR: for a single conventional project, the IRR rule and the NPV rule agree.

Check C3
For a conventional project that pays out first and receives later (such as project A in Figure 3-1), as long as the cost of capital is below its IRR, its NPV must be positive.
Think: how does a conventional project's NPV change with the discount rate? How many times does its NPV curve cross the horizontal axis?

Pitfalls of the IRR

Section titled “Pitfalls of the IRR”

The IRR is simple and easy to understand, but it gives wrong answers in these cases:

  • Mutually exclusive projects: when only one can be chosen, do not pick the one with the higher IRR. If projects differ in scale or in the timing of their cash flows, the IRR ranking and the NPV ranking can be opposite (as for the two projects in Figure 3-1). A project that recovers cash early has an NPV that is less sensitive to the discount rate; a project that recovers cash late has a larger NPV at low rates and a smaller one at high rates.
  • Multiple IRRs: if the cash flows change sign more than once (for example, a large cleanup cost at the end), the NPV profile may cross the axis several times, giving several IRRs or none at all (Exercises Question 2).
  • Borrowing-type projects: if money is received first and paid later (for example, payment in advance), the IRR is the cost of borrowing, and the project should be accepted only if the IRR is below the cost of capital.
  • A cost of capital that varies with maturity: if cash flows in different years call for different discount rates (3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates), there is no single hurdle to compare the IRR with.

In these cases NPV still gives the right answer. In practice the IRR is often used for communication, but decisions should rest on NPV.

Check C4
In Figure 3-1, project B's IRR (about 14.76%) is below project A's (about 17.21%). Only one of the two can be chosen, and the cost of capital is 5%. Which should be chosen?
A higher IRR does not mean a larger NPV. When only one project can be chosen, compare which creates more value at the cost of capital.
How fast a project pays back ignores the cash flows after payback, and ignores discounting.
Only one can be chosen; when both NPVs are positive, you still have to compare which is larger.

Other methods

Section titled “Other methods”

The payback period is the time it takes for cumulative cash flows to recover the initial investment. It is simple and reflects liquidity, but it has two flaws: it ignores the time value of money, and it ignores all cash flows after the payback period, so it favors short-term projects and rejects projects that are very valuable over the long run.

When funds are limited and not every positive-NPV project can be done (capital rationing), one can use the profitability index, the NPV divided by the initial investment −C0-C_0−C0​:

PI=NPV−C0\text{PI} = \frac{\text{NPV}}{-C_0}PI=−C0​NPV​

Choosing projects from the highest PI down until the budget runs out makes the total NPV as large as possible (Exercises Question 4). This is only an approximation: when projects cannot be split, one must also compare the total NPV of different combinations.

Check C5
A project with a shorter payback period always has a larger NPV.
Think: how does the payback method treat cash flows after the payback date? Does it discount?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • NPV =∑tCt(1+r)t= \sum_t \frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}=∑t​(1+r)tCt​​; accept if positive, and among mutually exclusive projects choose the largest NPV. The discount rate is the expected return on investments of the same risk: the cost of capital.
  • Include only incremental cash flows: exclude sunk costs; include opportunity costs, side effects, working capital and taxes; keep nominal and real consistent.
  • The IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero. For a single conventional project the IRR rule agrees with the NPV rule; for mutually exclusive projects, cash flows that change sign more than once, borrowing-type projects and a cost of capital that varies with maturity, the IRR can mislead.
  • Payback ignores time value and later cash flows; under capital rationing the profitability index gives an approximate ranking.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A project brings cash flows of 100 a year for 3 years, stated in today's prices (real). The nominal cost of capital is 8% and expected inflation 3%. (a) What is the present value of the cash flows? (b) An analyst discounts these cash flows at 8% directly. What does he get? What is wrong, and does he under- or overstate the value?
Question 2 ★
A mine: invest 100 today, receive 230 in year 1, and pay 132 for environmental cleanup in year 2. (a) With x=1+IRRx = 1 + \text{IRR}x=1+IRR, write NPV = 0 as a quadratic equation and find all the IRRs. (b) For what range of the cost of capital is the project worth doing? Why does "accept if the IRR exceeds the cost of capital" make no sense here?
Question 3 ★
The cost of capital is 10%, and there are two mutually exclusive projects: X invests 10 today and receives 15 in a year (IRR 50%); Y invests 1000 today and receives 1200 in a year (IRR 20%). (a) Which should be chosen? (b) Compute the IRR of the incremental cash flows from "switching from X to Y". Why does it also give the right choice?
Question 4
The budget is 100, and projects cannot be split: P1 invests 100 with NPV 20; P2 invests 50 with NPV 15; P3 invests 50 with NPV 12. (a) Which projects should be done? (b) If P3 needs 60 instead, how does the answer change? What limitation of ranking by profitability index does this show?
Question 5
A machine costs 1000 today and is depreciated straight-line over 5 years (200 a year); the corporate tax rate is 21% and the cost of capital 10%. (a) What is the present value of the tax saved each year because of depreciation? (b) If tax law allowed the whole 1000 to be deducted in the first year, would the present value of the tax savings be larger or smaller? Why?
